overview: An LDR (also called a photoresistor or CdS cell) is about as simple as sensors get: its resistance changes based on how much light hits it — high resistance in the dark, low resistance in bright light. It has no polarity, no datasheet timing protocol, and no digital interface at all; it's a passive component, not a smart sensor. To actually read it with a microcontroller's analog input, it has to be wired into a voltage divider with a fixed resistor, so light level shows up as a changing voltage rather than a directly readable resistance.
simpleSummary: A simple part whose resistance changes with light — bright light lets more current through.

specifications.responseTime: Slow compared to photodiodes/phototransistors (tens to hundreds of ms)
specifications.wiring: Requires a voltage-divider resistor to produce a readable analog voltage
specifications.polarity: None — it's a passive resistor, can be wired either way

pinMap.name: Terminal 1
pinMap.function: One leg of the resistive element. Paired with a fixed resistor (commonly 10kΩ) to form a voltage divider read by an analog input.
pinMap.voltageRange: Passive component — voltage depends on divider circuit
pinMap.gotcha: By itself, an LDR doesn't produce a voltage — it just changes resistance. A common beginner mistake is wiring it directly to an analog pin expecting a reading, without the divider resistor.

pinMap.name: Terminal 2
pinMap.function: Other leg of the resistive element — no polarity, interchangeable with Terminal 1.

useCases.title: Automatic night light
useCases.scenario: Turn on an LED automatically once ambient light drops below a threshold.

useCases.title: Light-following robot
useCases.scenario: Compare readings from two or more LDRs to steer a robot toward (or away from) a light source.

useCases.title: Ambient-light-aware display brightness
useCases.scenario: Adjust a display or LED strip's brightness based on room lighting conditions.

oftenUpgradedTo: A dedicated digital light sensor (e.g. BH1750) for calibrated lux readings over I2C
